https://focustaiwan.tw:443/culture/20260.text: Taiwan's students shine at international Biology, Chemistry Olympiads Taipei/Vilnius, July 19 (CNA) Taiwanese students won four gold medals at the International Biology Olympiad and three golds and one silver at the International Chemistry Olympiad, ranking first and third, respectively, in gold medal tallies, the Ministry of Education (MOE) said Sunday. At the 37th International Biology Olympiad in Vilnius, Lithuania, Taiwan swept all four gold medals available to its team, with Yao I-keng (姚亦耕) from Taipei Municipal Chien Kuo High School (CKHS) placing fourth individually. Chan Wei-chun (詹緯濬), also of CKHS, placed fifth overall, while Chen Yu-chen (陳語晨) of Taipei First Girls High School ranked 18th and Hsu Ting-jui (許庭睿) of Taichung Municipal Taichung First Senior High School (TCFSH) finished 19th. Taiwan's four-gold haul topped the medal table among 78 participating countries and 302 contestants. The awards ceremony was held Saturday (local time), according to an MOE news release. Taiwan's representative to Lithuania, Constance Wang (王雪虹), attended the ceremony and conveyed congratulations from President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) and Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴), the Taiwanese Representative Office in Lithuania said. Meanwhile, at the 58th International Chemistry Olympiad in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, Taiwan won three gold medals and one silver, ranking third in the number of gold medals, according to a separate MOE news release. Gold medals went to Fang I-chen (方怡宸) from CKHS, Chang Chen-jui (張宸睿) of Kaohsiung Municipal Kaohsiung Senior High School and Fan I-yang (范奕揚) from TCFSH, while Cheng Ping-hao (鄭秉皓) of National Experimental High School at Hsinchu Science Park earned a silver medal. The competition involved 363 students from 92 countries, according to the MOE. Under Ministry of Education (MOE) regulations, Taiwanese students who win gold, silver, or bronze medals at international academic Olympiads receive cash awards of NT$200,000 (US$6,169), NT$100,000, and NT$50,000, respectively, from the ministry. They are also eligible for direct admission to relevant university departments or recommendation-based admission to any academic program. The Lies that Frame the Narrative For the past few years you have been asked to believe a narrative about nuclear nonproliferation which is not true. That’s not to say that those spreading the lies are aware that they are not speaking the truth; often they are simply repeating, or reporting, what they have been told, what they believe to be true. The most common claim is that Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons in exchange for territorial security guarantees and after February 2022 the West is now obligated to defend “Ukrainian” territory. The second claim is that South Africa gave up its nuclear weapons and weapons program voluntarily in order to be welcomed back into collegial relations with the rest of the world. Neither story is true. Both are designed to reinforce the importance of the Western security umbrella, but from different angles. Since the outbreak of open hostilities between Russia and Ukraine in February 2022, a mythical take on the 1994 Budapest Memorandum has been used by Ukraine and its supporters to demand military and other support. At the time of the collapse of the Soviet Union, approximately 1,900 strategic nuclear warheads were located in what had suddenly become sovereign Ukrainian territory. The Budapest Memorandum, signed by the Russian Federation, Ukraine, the United States, and the United Kingdom, arranged for the return of those warheads in exchange for political assurances regarding Ukraine’s territorial integrity. The Memorandum is not and never was a binding treaty and at most it demanded political “assurances” (and in the Russian and Ukrainian version “guarantees”), not arms and armies. More critical, however, is the fact that the warheads were not Ukrainian and were never under Ukrainian command and control. Despite robust efforts to gain access to the launch codes and other authorities which would allow for use of the weapons, the Ukrainians never succeeded and the warheads were unusable. The weapons were Soviet and the launch authority and all of its complexities lay in the Russian Federation. While some scholars have argued that it may have been feasible for Ukraine to eventually hack into the system, the reality is that they tried and failed and then made a deal. Only after Ukrainian failure did they accept the Budapest Memorandum, returning to Russia what was never Ukrainian. A state does not exchange a functioning deterrent for a non-binding agreement, but it will give up custody of someone else’s weapons for one. Returning a weapon you cannot use is not the myth of sacrifice Ukraine and its supporters present. Thus, the Budapest Memorandum proves a different story: political assurances from great powers are nonbinding. Ukraine’s borders continue to shrink and there is nothing assured or guaranteed by the West regarding their return to pre-war boundaries. The false version of the story, however, works very well for its purposes. For Ukraine it converts its sacrifice, the return of the nuclear weapons, into a debt owed to it by the West. After all, if Ukraine voluntarily gave up its weapons of mass destruction based on a promise that it would be protected from invasion, and then Russia broke the promise by invading, the West must follow through with support, both military and financial. For advocates of Ukrainian membership in NATO, the argument is extended further: if the obligations of the Budapest Memorandum can be ignored, then Ukraine must be admitted into NATO by treaty so that Article 5 can apply and make legal and official what the Memorandum failed to do. For those who advocate aggression against Russia, the story makes Western military and financial assistance in Ukraine’s fight a moral obligation and a debt to be repaid. However, as Ukraine never controlled the weapons at all, the Budapest Memorandum was never a trade, it was a Russian promise of forbearance and a Western promise of assurance, both broken decades later. The false story is a simplistic tale which attempts to use the Budapest Memorandum to make a moral argument in lieu of NATO’s Article 5 requirement to defend a partner. Given that Ukraine is not a member of NATO, Russia did not need to fear a NATO response. The lie about Ukrainian nonproliferation is designed as an end-around in order to make a Western military response a moral requirement. South African unilateral nuclear disarmament is often presented as a “feel good story” in which a rogue state saw reason, ended its program, along with its apartheid governance, and was welcomed into the community of nations. The timing and trajectory are correct, but the reasons behind the decision show a different moral to the story. As South African whites-only rule was drawing to a close in 1989, President F.W. de Klerk ordered the dismantling of its nuclear program, which at that time consisted of six completed nuclear weapons with a seventh under construction. In February 1990, the ban against the African National Congress (ANC) was lifted. The weapons and program were gone by 1991, although the official announcement of this was not public until March 1993, during negotiations regarding the official transfer of power to the ANC. The official story was that the weapons were no longer needed given the end of the Cold War, the withdrawal of Cuban forces from Angola, and a long-delayed peace settlement ending South Africa’s conflict in Namibia. All of those details are true; however, the decision to disarm was not from external persuasion or events, it was from the uniquely South African transition from the apartheid era to majority black rule. The Afrikaner government never intended to hand a functioning nuclear arsenal to its former adversaries; they disarmed for the same racist reasons which underpinned their regime: they were not going to usher the ANC into the world’s smallest club, the nuclear powers. This second misleading myth reinforces a completely different narrative. It tells the story of the only example of a nuclear armed state disarming out of conviction, the only case in which institutional norms, pressure, and inducement produced nuclear disarmament, and thus is the institutional justification for the pressures since applied to Iraq, Libya, Iran, and North Korea. The entire system of sanctions, inspections, and the carrot of admission into respectable company, are all based on the South African example. A true account of South Africa’s motives eliminates the one example and demonstrates that the track record of persuaded disarmament has no successes whatsoever. Both anecdotes serve the greater narrative which is that a nation should accept the Western security umbrella, its nuclear shield, rather than its own. Unilateral disarmament brings a nation under that umbrella. Disarmament without that protection invites invasion. Should a nation try to create its own nuclear deterrent, it will be punished, sanctioned, and even attacked, as demonstrated in the public justification for the US and Israeli attacks on Iran in 2025 and 2026. Once both anecdotes are correctly interpreted a very different message is revealed: the sole example of a state surrendering functioning nuclear weapons under its control was when the ruling regime would lose control of them anyway. Critically, no state on Earth is in this position. There is no government for which abandonment of a functioning nuclear deterrent is preferable to the “guarantees” and “assurances” of someone else’s security umbrella. II. An Eroding Deterrence Credible nuclear deterrence is often thought to be ironclad (the example of North Korea springs immediately to mind), and from the early days of the Cold War, no state with nuclear weapons was invaded and none were overthrown. Deterrence worked. That is, until the end of 2022. In December 2022 the conflict in Ukraine took a significant and unprecedented escalation with a strike against the Engels strategic bomber base, deep inside Russia. This is one third of Russia’s “nuclear triad”: the air, land, and sea-based strategic nuclear deterrent. It would prove to be anything but an isolated incident. It was followed by the May 2024 attacks on Russian over-the-horizon radar installations at Armavir and Orsk. These are critical components of Russia’s early warning system designed to provide Moscow early warning of incoming American (or other) missile launches and to provide Russian leadership time to consider the launching of a counterstrike. Elimination of those installations reduces the time available to assess the situation and increases the likelihood of a false-positive and thus a mistaken second-strike. These radars are not used in any way in the Ukraine war. Blinding them was a massive escalation and risk, for Moscow had published in 2020 the conditions in which a nuclear retaliation would be justified, and destroying these radars was among them. Then came Operation Spiderweb, the audacious 1 June 2025 attack on multiple Russian airfields across the country. Ukraine publicly took credit for the operation in which specially modified trucks simultaneously released hordes of drones which targeted and destroyed a number of Tu-95 strategic bombers. While the degree of success is hotly debated, it is indisputable that Ukraine, with clear Western assistance, carried out an attack against Russia’s nuclear bombers, taking advantage of Russian compliance with their New START treaty obligations to house them in open air. Ten months earlier, Ukrainian forces, with significant assistance from their Western military sponsors, invaded sovereign Russian territory in Kursk, an action unthinkable during the Cold War. None of these attacks touched Russia’s land-based or submarine-based nuclear capabilities and Russia’s second-strike capabilities were barely impacted. In none of these examples was Ukraine or its partners deterred by Russian possession of the world’s greatest nuclear arsenal. Why not? The answer is uncomfortable and it carries the implication that nuclear weapons are more likely to be used than not. Russian deterrence failed, and these attacks have led to escalation, which many have argued was precisely the objective. Every attack above, as well as many more, was met with a firm and at times overwhelming conventional response, including new and innovative weapons systems such as the jet-powered Geran-4 drones (based on the original Iranian Shaheds) and the still somewhat mysterious Oreshnik. However, possession of the world’s greatest nuclear arsenal did not prevent these attacks and did not produce a nuclear response. This leads to the inescapable conclusion that a nuclear deterrent deters regime change operations but nothing more, and even here deterrence has failed. Strategic weapons have become too powerful and mutually assured destruction has set the stakes too high, thus if everyone knows that a country is unlikely to end life as we know it, the weapons fail to deter anything but the end of the world. Unless, of course, smaller, tactical nuclear weapons are brought into the equation and normalized for use. Which is exactly what is happening now. III. A New Threshold Moscow was the first to publicly address the problem that if strategic nuclear weapons deter only attempts to destroy the state, lower levels of deterrence required the threat of a weapon its adversaries not only feared, but feared would be used. The first step was to officially lower the threshold required for a nuclear response, published in November 2024. https://yle.fi/a/74-20245189.text: Helsinki District Court on Tuesday began hearing the case against two crew members of the cargo ship Fitburg, which is suspected of damaging cables in the Gulf of Finland last New Year's Eve. The preliminary investigation uncovered evidence that the Fitburg dragged a broken anchor along the seabed for at least 130 kilometers until Finnish authorities stopped the vessel. The two defendants in the case are the Russian captain, Andrei Maksimenko , and an Azerbaijani bosun. A bosun is a senior petty officer in charge of a ship's deck crew and rigging. They face at least two and a half years in prison if found guilty on the charges of aggravated sabotage and aggravated interference with communications networks. Both men have denied the charges. According to prosecutors, the Fitburg damaged two telecommunications cables in Estonia's exclusive economic zone, with some of the damage also occurring in Finnish territorial waters. This could have had serious consequences for the functioning of telecommunications, electricity, and gas networks in Finland, the prosecutor told the court. Finnish authorities took control of the ship in the immediate aftermath of the incident on New Year's Eve. The vessel was en route from Russia to Israel, according to the ship-tracking website MarineTraffic. At the time, it was sailing under the flag of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines — a commonly-used so-called "flag of convenience", which allows a shipowner from one country to fly under the flag of another. Open image viewer The Fitburg was transferred by Finnish authorities under official escort to Kantvik harbour, near the municipality of Kirkkonummi in southern Finland, on New Year's Eve. Image: Poliisi The case has striking similarities with the Eagle S, which is also suspected of damaging undersea cables in the Gulf of Finland — a year earlier, over Christmas 2024. In October 2025, the district court ruled that Finland does not have jurisdiction and dismissed that case, but the Appeal Court overturned that decision at the end of last month and returned it to the district court. Henrik Ringbom , a Professor of Maritime Law at Åbo Akademi in Turku, told Yle that the district court's decision in the Eagle S case was "surprising" as it could set a precedent for any potential similar incidents in international waters. "In practice, it would mean free game – come on in, as long as you're outside the territorial waters boundary, we won't do anything," Ringbom explained. The issue of jurisdiction is likely to be a key factor in the Fitburg case as well, with the legal counsel for the Azerbaijani bosun telling Yle just before the hearing that this case should not be heard in a Finnish court.
